title: Returning Values
description: Functions that work something out and hand the answer back.

items: A printed value is shown once. You cannot add to it, compare it or save it.
A function that **returns** its result hands back a value you can do anything with.
Two changes: swap `void` for the type you hand back, and use `return` to hand it back. `main`'s `return 0;` has done this all along.

parts.label: return type
parts.note: A promise: this function hands back an `int`.

parts.label: name
parts.note: What you write to call it.

parts.label: parameters
parts.note: Two ints come in, each with its own type.

steps.note: To work out the right side of `=`, C++ must call `add`. It jumps in.
The parameters arrive with the arguments.
`a + b` is 7. `return` hands 7 back and leaves the function.
The call is replaced by 7, exactly as if you had typed `7`. `a` and `b` are gone.
`add(10, 5)` runs and becomes 15, used straight away.

content.title: Watch the value come back
content.outro: A returned value can be stored, printed or used in a bigger calculation. By the time the rest of the line runs, it is just a value.

content.question: What does this print?
content.explain: `twice(4)` hands back 8, so the line becomes `8 + 1`, which is 9.

items: `return` does two jobs: it hands the value back, and it **finishes** the function there and then.
C++ lets you write lines after a `return`, but they can never run. They are just clutter.
Leaving early is handy: deal with special cases first, with no `else` needed.

steps.note: Hand back `"A"` and leave. The lines below never run this time.
The call became `"A"`, so it prints.
Print it. Three returns in the function, exactly one taken each time.

content.title: Watch return leave early
content.outro: No `else` anywhere: once a `return` runs, nothing below it can. Try `grade(12)` and it reaches `return "Fail"`.

content.caption: A `void` function can use `return;` with no value. It just means "I am finished", like `break` for a whole function. A guard at the top deals with bad input first, so the rest can trust it.

content.question: What does this print?
content.explain: 50 makes the `if` true, so it returns `"big"`. 5 skips the `if` and reaches `return "small"`.

content.value: A function that promises a value must deliver one however it is called. You must keep this rule yourself: C++ does not enforce it strictly.

items.title: Builds, but is broken
items.text: `grade(12)` runs off the closing brace with nothing to hand back.

items.title: Safe
items.text: Every route through the function ends in a `return`.

content.title: A missing return
content.caption: Fix: a final `return` outside every `if`, or finish the chain with an `else` that returns.

content.value: g++ builds the broken version, at most with the warning `control reaches end of non-void function`. What happens then is **undefined**: C++ promises nothing. Garbage, an empty answer or a crash, and it can change between runs.
content.title: Undefined behaviour

content.question: A returning function sometimes gives nonsense. What should you look for first?
content.explain: If one route through the function skips every `return`, the result is undefined. A missing return is one of the first things to check.

content.value: Functions That Answer Yes or No

items: A function can return a `bool`. That lets you give a test a name.
Name them as questions: `isEven`, `isPrime`, `isValid`, `hasPaid`, `canVote`. Then `if (canVote(age))` reads like English.
`cout << boolalpha;` prints `true` and `false`. Without it, a `bool` prints as `1` or `0`.

content.caption: `isEven` has no `if`: `n % 2 == 0` already **is** true or false, so return it directly.

items.title: The long way
items.text: Four lines to produce a value you already had.

items.title: The neat way
items.text: Says exactly the same thing in one line.

items: Returns plus the loops from Module 5 make a toolbox. Each function does one job, hands back one answer, and can be tested alone.
`digitSum` and `reverseDigits` divide `n` down to nothing. That is safe: `n` is their own copy.
`factorial` returns a `long long`: an `int` overflows after 12!. Pick a return type big enough for every answer.

content.caption: Tools like these plus a menu are this module's project. You have already seen the hard part.

content.title: isPrime(91) leaves early
content.caption: The final `return true` is only reached if the loop runs out without finding a divisor.

content.value: One function, one job, one thing returned. A `return` hands back only one value. Need two? The next lesson shows a C++ way.
content.title: One job each

practice.question: Write square(int n) that returns n times n, then use a loop in main to print the squares of 1 to 5.
Write largest(int a, int b) that returns the bigger of the two. The conditional operator makes it one line.
Write isValidScore(int score) that returns true only for 0 to 100, then use it in an if to accept or reject a number.
This compiles, but category(75) hands back nothing at all. Fix it so every possible age gets an answer.

quiz.question: What do you change to make a function hand a value back?
options: Just add a return at the end
Replace void with the type of the value, and use return
quiz.explain: The return type is the promise and `return` keeps it.

quiz.question: What does `return` do besides handing back a value?
options: It ends the function immediately, so nothing below it runs
quiz.explain: That is why early returns need no `else`, and why lines written after a return never run.

quiz.question: A `string` function reaches its closing brace without a `return`. What happens?
options: The result is undefined: you might get garbage or a crash
The program always refuses to compile
quiz.explain: g++ builds it, at most with a warning. Every path through a non-void function must end in a return, and keeping that rule is your job.

quiz.question: What is the tidy way to write `isEven`?
quiz.explain: The comparison is already a bool, so returning it directly says the same thing in one line.

quiz.question: What does a bare `return;` do in a void function?
options: Leaves the function early without handing anything back
quiz.explain: It is the function-level `break`, and it is ideal for a guard at the top that rejects impossible input.
